papers.title_in_file: Exploring Quantum Perceptron and Quantum Neural Network structures with a teacher-student scheme
papers.version_note: arXiv:2105.01477v2 (25 Nov 2021). The text layer holds the paper once. Page numbers in anchors are the printed page footers (page 1 carries no footer).
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that introduces a teacher-student scheme to compare the expressive power of a quantum perceptron (QP) architecture, deeper QNNs built from QPs, and the data re-uploading (RU) architecture on two-qubit, two-input circuits.

existing.value: The authors state that the aim of the work is to introduce a teacher-student scheme that could systematically compare any QNN architectures and evaluate their relative expressive power.
quotes: The aim of this work is to introduce a teacher-student scheme that could systematically compare any QNN architectures and evaluate their relative expressive power.
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own aim and setup.

existing.value: The authors state that the deep structures built from quantum perceptrons only increase the expressivity of a model if the data are uploaded several times.
quotes: we showed that the deep structures that can be built with QPs only increase the expressivity of a model if the data are uploaded several times.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result of simulations from one study on one two-input, two-qubit data encoding; no proof is given.
existing.reader_inference: The evidence is the comparison of the single-perceptron circuit, the deep QP circuit and the two-perceptron network in the paper's Fig. 4 and Fig. 5, with loss curves and prediction maps for one example each. The paper reports no repeat statistics for those three circuits.

existing.note: The paper makes this statement inside Section 5.1, titled Toy model, which it introduces as an illustrative example, and it says 'Even for this toy example' about the four metrics. The scope is the toy model: the RU and QP circuits of Fig. 1, two-dimensional inputs, and 10 random initializations of the teacher. The anchor is also corrected: the passage is Section 5.1 on p.5 (printed page footer), not Section 5 p.6. The QP student is not at zero error on the RU teacher: its average relative entropy is 0.247 against 0.001 for the RU student.
existing.value: The authors report, for their toy model (an illustrative teacher-student example with 10 random initializations of the teacher), that the RU architecture can generate and learn more complex output distributions than the QP: it can learn all the data sets generated by the QP with almost zero loss and relative entropy, while the QP is not able to learn the data sets provided by the RU.
quotes: Here, we will elaborate the notion of the teacher-student scheme with an illustrative example.
We generated 10 different data sets by randomly initializing the teacher
In conclusion, the RU architecture can generate and learn more complex output distributions than the QP.
It can learn all the data sets generated by the QP with almost zero loss and relative entropy.
On the contrary, the QP is not able to learn the data sets provided by the RU.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result of simulations from one study on a toy example.
existing.reader_inference: The generality of the sentence 'the RU architecture can generate and learn more complex output distributions than the QP' rests on one toy configuration (QP and RU circuits of Fig. 1 with one and two pairs of encoding gates). Section 5.2 repeats the ordering for a deeper RU teacher, but the accuracy score there is about 0.8 for both students.

assertions.value: The authors state that the teacher generates labels for a fixed set of two dimensional inputs on a grid with each coordinate in [−π, π], using several random initializations of the processing-gate parameters, and that the ancilla measurement outcome is used as the model prediction.
quotes: with 2 dimensional input vectors x = {x1, x2} on a grid xi ∈ [−π, π].
we choose several random initializations for the parameters w of the processing gates
We use the measurement outcomes of the ancilla qubit as the model predictions yk of the input data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 states the paper's own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the teacher predictions take continuous values yk in [−1, 1] given by the measurement outcome, that they also generate binary valued labels as the sign of yk, and that the teachers with binary labels focus more on the basic characteristics of the data structures while the ones with continuous labels also care for the details.
quotes: The predictions have continuous values yk ∈ [−1, 1] given by the outcome of the measurement
but we also generate binary valued labels by choosing ybkinary = sign(yk).
The teachers with binary labels focus more on the basic characteristics of the data structures, while the ones with continuous labels also care for the details.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 defines the label types of the paper's own setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that they encode a two dimensional input with the gates Rx(x1) and Rx(x2) on two distinct qubits (angle encoding), use the same encoding for all models to have a fair comparison, and realize the trainable part with the single qubit rotations Rot(φ, θ, ω) = Rz(ω)Ry(θ)Rz(φ) and controlled-Z gates.
quotes: encode the data to the circuit with the gates U (x) = Rx(x1) ⊗ Rx(x2) applied on two distinct qubits
Throughout this work, we use the same encoding for all models to have a fair comparison.
The trainable part of the perceptron is realized by parameterized single qubit rotations Rot(φ, θ, ω) = Rz(ω)Ry(θ)Rz(φ) and controlled-Z gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 defines the encoding and the processing gates used in every experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that for classification with two labels they measure one qubit in a single direction, for example the Z direction, and that the cost function is minimized during the training.
quotes: we measure one qubit in a single direction, e.g. in Z direction
which is minimized during the training.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 defines the readout and the training objective of the paper's own models.

assertions.value: The authors state that a hidden quantum perceptron consists of a parameterized processing gate, a (multi)controlled NOT gate that activates another ancillary system and a deferred measurement, that this architecture builds deep structures coherently with the ancillary systems measured at the very end of the circuit, and that the idea is that the deferred measurement introduces the required nonlinearity between the layers.
quotes: the hidden perceptron itself consists of a parameterized processing gate U (w), a (multi)controlled NOT gate that activates another ancillary system and a deferred measurement.
This architecture allows one to build deep structures in a coherent way and the ancillary systems can be measured at the very end of the circuit.
The idea is that because of this deferred measurement the required nonlinearity is still introduced between the layers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 defines the hidden-perceptron architecture that the later experiments test.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence 'The idea is that' states the hypothesis the paper then tests; the paper's own results (Section 5.3) do not support it.

assertions.value: The authors state that both the original binary and the later continuous versions of the quantum perceptron of Tacchino et al. need the basis encoding, which requires many qubits, that they use the angle encoding to avoid this, and that this allows for continuous inputs and weights.
quotes: Both methods though need the basis encoding which requires many qubits to encode the data.
To avoid this, we use the angle encoding introduced earlier in this section.
This allows for continuous inputs and weights.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 states how the paper's QP differs from the cited original.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [18], that the non-linear activations are introduced with dissipative units where ancillary qubits form the output layer while the qubits from the input layers are discarded.
quotes: The non-linear activations are introduced with dissipative units where ancillary qubits form the output layer, while the qubits from the input layers are discarded [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [18].

assertions.value: The authors state that in the re-uploading architecture each data dependent unitary is followed by a parameterized unitary with trainable parameters, and that because of the repeated application of Li = U (w)U (x) to the circuit the scheme is called data re-uploading.
quotes: Each of these data dependent unitaries is followed by a parameterized unitary U (w) with trainable parameters w.
Because of the repeated application of Li = U (w)U (x) to the circuit, this scheme is called data re-uploading.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 defines the re-uploading architecture used in the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to make the two perceptron models more comparable, the RU model also uses a multi-controlled NOT gate to activate an ancilla qubit exactly like in the QP and the same cost function.
quotes: we also use a multi-controlled NOT gate to activate an ancilla qubit exactly like in QP.
We also use the same cost function from Eq. (1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 states the paper's own comparison setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the notion of depth is not as clearly defined for the re-uploading scheme as it is for the QP, and that it is known, citing [29], that more layers of re-uploading lead to better expressivity of the model although there is no clear classical analog to this.
quotes: for the re-uploading scheme as it is for the QP.
It is known that more layers of re-uploading lead to better expressivity of the model [29]
but there is no clear classical analog to this.
assertions.certainty_reason: The expressivity claim is a result the paper attributes to other work [29].

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantitative comparison between student and teacher outputs uses the information divergence (Kullback–Leibler divergence or relative entropy) between prediction maps, with the predicted labels offset and re-normalized so they can be read as probabilities, and that the metric is close to zero when the two distributions are similar.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.2 Notion of student, Eq. (2), pp.4-5
quotes: we use the information divergence (Kullback–Leibler divergence or relative entropy)
To interpret the predicted labels yk as probabilities, we offset and re-normalize them
Here, we are interested in the average rel-
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 defines the metric the results depend on.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'close to zero when similar' clause comes from the sentence 'When the two distributions are similar, the value of the rela-/tive entropy is close to zero' split by a line break; it is not quoted here because of the hyphenated break.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the student is trained with the binary valued labels the percentage of correctly predicted labels is computed and called the accuracy score, and that to identify a good or bad student all the tools (prediction maps, loss, accuracy and relative entropy) should be taken into account.
quotes: the percentage of the correctly predicted labels can be computed. We refer to this as the accuracy score
good/bad student all these tools should be taken into account.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 defines the accuracy score and the evaluation protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that the teacher-student scheme avoids training on arbitrary data sets, allows comparison of the learning capacity of different models directly via the loss, the prediction map, the accuracy and the relative entropy, that artificial data sets could possibly favour one of the architectures, and that the scheme could be used for any circuits.
quotes: This way, we avoid training on arbitrary data sets and allow to compare the learning capacity of different models directly via the loss, the prediction map, the accuracy and the relative entropy between the prediction maps.
that could possibly favour one of the architectures.
but the scheme could be used for any circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the benefit of the scheme; the paper tests it only on the QP and RU circuits.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not test whether a teacher-student data set is less biased than a fixed one such as the circle data set; the appendix instead shows that labelling and input normalization change the results.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for the RU teacher in the toy model, the QP student does not learn the inner structure (circles) at the left and right sides of the teacher prediction map, that the RU student reproduces the teacher almost perfectly, and that the RU student achieves a much lower loss in the shown example.
quotes: where the Student - QP does not learn the inner structure (circles) at the left and right sides of the prediction map of the teacher.
The Student - RU reproduces almost perfectly the teacher as expected, since they have the same circuit architecture.
where Student - Re-uploading achieves a much lower loss.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one example in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The loss values appear only in the figure, which the text layer does not carry.

assertions.value: The authors report that training the students on the binary labels of the RU teacher gives an accuracy score approximately 0.9 for the RU student compared to 0.8 for the QP student, and state that both students have a high accuracy score because the topology of the prediction maps with binary labels is very similar.
quotes: we reach the accuracy score approximately equal to 0.9 compared to 0.8 for the QP.
Both students have a high accuracy score, since the topology of the prediction maps of the students and the teacher with binary labels are very similar
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one example in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, over 10 data sets generated by randomly initializing the RU teacher, the average relative entropy is 0.247 for the QP student and 0.001 for the RU student.
quotes: We generated 10 different data sets by randomly initializing the teacher
the average relative entropy over all prediction maps which is equal to 0.247 and 0.001 for the Student - QP and the Student - RU, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study over 10 teacher initializations.
assertions.reader_inference: No spread or error bar over the 10 initializations is reported.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the RU teacher the average loss of the QP student (black dashed line) is larger than the loss of the single example shown in the prediction map, and that the RU student shows good convergence for all data sets generated by the teacher.
quotes: The average loss for the Student - QP (black dashed line) is larger than the single example shown in the prediction map (black solid line)
The Student - RU shows good convergence (blue dashed line) for all data sets generated by the teacher
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The RU student has the same architecture as the RU teacher, so good convergence is the expected case; the paper says as much.

assertions.value: The authors state that the loss captures better the global differences in the prediction (a general off-set of the whole prediction maps), while the relative entropy captures local differences in the maps.
quotes: the loss captures better the global differences in the prediction (i.e. a general off-set of the whole prediction maps), while the relative entropy captures local differences in the maps
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper gives no test of it beyond the toy example.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the QP as the teacher the average loss of both students converges to similar low values, both students have an accuracy score of 0.9, and the average relative entropy is approximately zero for both students (0.0002 for the QP and 0.0013 for the RU).
quotes: The average loss for both students converges to similar low values
we have a high accuracy score 0.9 of both students
approximately equal to zero for both students ( 0.0002 for the QP and 0.0013 for the RU).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results with the QP as the teacher suggest that the QP generates simpler data structures and that both architectures can learn them.
quotes: These results suggest that the QP generates simpler data structures and both architectures can learn them.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's inference from one toy experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the difficulty of deciding whether a student is good or bad means one should take into consideration all the tools together: the prediction maps, the accuracy score, and the average loss and relative entropy.
quotes: one should take under consideration all the different tools introduced earlier (the prediction maps,
the accuracy score, the (average) loss and relative entropy) to characterize the performance of the students.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's methodological recommendation.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself shows a case (Section 5.2) where the accuracy score is about equal for both students while the loss and the prediction maps differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that the more complex teacher is a deep re-uploading architecture with four pairs of encoding gates, whereas the QP and RU students can learn with one and two pairs of encoding unitaries, respectively.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 A more complex teacher, Fig. 3, p.6
quotes: re-uploading architecture in Fig. 3 (Teacher) with many repetitions of the encoding gates.

the teacher with four pairs of encoding gates generate a more complex data structure compared to the ones that the student of the QP and RU can learn with one and two pairs of encoding unitaries, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.2 states the paper's own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the deep teacher the RU student learns the basic features of the teacher architecture while the QP student learns a very simplified version of the data structure.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 A more complex teacher, Fig. 3, p.6
quotes: The Student - RU learns the basic features of the teacher
contrary to the Student - QP which learns a very simpliﬁed version of the data structure.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one characteristic example in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that training the students on the binary valued outputs of the deep teacher gives accuracy scores approximately 0.8 for both students, and state that the accuracy score therefore does not allow one to determine which student learns the teacher more accurately.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 A more complex teacher, p.6 (Fig. 9, p.10)
quotes: we reach accuracy scores approximately equal to 0.8 for both students
Therefore, the accuracy score does not allow to determine which student learns the teacher more accurately.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that over 10 realizations of the deep teacher the average loss curve of the RU student is much lower than the average loss curve of the QP student.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 A more complex teacher, Fig. 3, p.6
quotes: the average loss curve for Student - RU (blue dashed line) over 10 realizations of the teacher is much lower than the average loss curve of Student - QP (black dashed line).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The loss values appear only in the figure, not in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the deep teacher the average relative entropy is 0.15 for the QP student and 0.11 for the RU student.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 A more complex teacher, p.6
quotes: the average relative entropy is equal to 0.15 and 0.11 for the Student - QP and the Student - RU, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The gap between 0.15 and 0.11 is small and no spread is reported, so the entropy result gives weak support for the ordering.

assertions.value: The authors report that adding four more processing gates to the QP student, each followed by CNOT entangling gates, did not improve the performance of the perceptron, and state that this suggests the structure of the circuit is not enough to simulate the data structure of the re-uploading perceptron as a teacher.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.3 Improving the QP, p.6; Appendix A 2, p.11
quotes: Therefore, we add four more processing gates to the Student - QP each followed by CNOT entangling gates
The performance of the perceptron though did not improve, suggesting that the structure of the circuit is not enough
does not improve the performance of the model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Sousa et al. [33], that eight single qubit unitaries and four entangling gates realize an arbitrary two qubit gate.
quotes: Sousa et. al. [33] show that eight single qubit unitaries and four entangling gates realize an arbitrary two qubit gate.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [33].

assertions.value: The authors report that the deep circuit built by using the output of one QP twice did not improve in performance, and state that this means the deferred measurement on the second ancilla is not enough to improve the performance of the architecture.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.3 Improving the QP, Fig. 4b and Fig. 5, p.6
quotes: instead of using the output of one QP twice as in Fig. 4b, we use two QP to form a QNN.
The performance of the circuit did not improve though (see Fig. 5), which means that the deferred measurement on the second ancilla is not enough to improve the performance of the architecture.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one circuit.
assertions.reader_inference: The negative result concerns one specific construction (one perceptron's output reused through two CNOT gates and CZ gates onto a third ancilla); it does not exclude other coherent deep QP constructions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the failure of the deep QP circuit shows that the formation of coherent deep QNN structures does not follow the classical analog of a classical deep NN, that is by stacking several perceptrons together.
quotes: This shows that the formation of coherent deep QNN structures does not follow the classical analog of a classical deep NN, i.e. by staking several perceptrons together.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's generalization from one tested circuit.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence generalizes from one tested construction to coherent deep QNNs in general.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum ffNN, which uses two QPs as building blocks of a QNN, shows improved learning capability and performs quite well, as suggested by the convergence to a low value of the loss curve, and state that this suggests the deferred measurement does not provide the necessary depth and shows the importance of re-uploading the data several times.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.3 Improving the QP, Fig. 4c and Fig. 5, p.6
quotes: This circuit shows improved learning capability and performs quite well as suggested by the convergence to a low value of the loss curve (see Fig.5).

suggests that the deferred measurement does not provide the necessary depth to the circuit and shows the importance of re-uploading the data several times to increase the performance of the architecture.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state in a figure caption that the eight-gate QP and the deep QP models have the same expressivity as the QP, contrary to the quantum ffNN, which performs better as the RU.
quotes: The models in (a) and (b) have the same expressivity with the QP, contrary to the quantum ffNN (c) which performs better as the RU
assertions.certainty_reason: A caption summary of empirical results from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Schuld et al. [29], that the complexity of the functions a circuit learns is determined by the number of times the encoding gates are applied, and that there is no difference whether the data are encoded vertically or horizontally.
quotes: The recent work of Schuld et. al. [29] shows that the complexity of the functions that a circuit learns is determined by the number of times that the encoding gates are applied.
They emphasize that there is no difference if the encoding data are introduced in a circuit vertically
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [29].

assertions.value: The authors state that the QNN of two QPs and the RU encode the data twice in a vertical or in a horizontal way respectively, regard the two architectures as equivalent in that sense with the prediction maps enhancing this claim, and note as suggested in [29] that the trainable circuit and measurement could affect the functions that can be approximated.
quotes: Both circuits encode the data twice in a vertical or in a horizontal way, respectively.
In that sense, the architectures of these two models are equivalent and the prediction maps enhance this claim.
But, as suggested in the work [29], the trainable circuit and measurement could affect the functions that can be approximated.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim supported by prediction maps and a cited result.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the two-QP quantum feed-forward network the average accuracy score is 0.84 and the average relative entropy is 0.098, compared to 0.9 and 0.0009 for the RU, and state these values differ significantly.
quotes: the average accuracy score is equal to 0.84 and the average relative entropy gives 0.098
different from the values of the RU in Fig. 1b (0.9 and 0.0009, respectively).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say which teacher produced these averages; read in context it appears to be the toy-model RU teacher.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QNN and the RU have similar performance but there are some qualitative differences between them due to the differences in the trainable part of the circuits, and that the average relative entropy calculation showed the trainable part of the circuit affects the functions that can be approximated.
quotes: there are some qualitative differences between them due to the differences at the trainable part of the circuits [29].
showed that the trainable part of the circuit affects the functions that can be approximated.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's inference from two average metrics of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The inference rests on one accuracy and one relative entropy average per circuit; the paper does not isolate the trainable part by an ablation.

assertions.value: The authors state that they compare the angle encoding with the encoding Rot(x1, x2, 0)H applied at each qubit by encoding 500 input data points from a circular data set without the processing unitaries, computing the probability vectors of the encoded states, and applying principal component analysis to convert them to two dimensional data sets.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.4 Role of the encoding, pp.7-8
quotes: Here, we want to compare the aforementioned angle encoding with the encoding Rot(x1, x2, 0)H applied at each qubit.
we encode 500 input data points {x1, x2} from the circular data set and create the probability vectors for each one of them for the different encodings.
We apply principle component analysis (PCA) on each one of the probability vectors which converts them to two dimensional data sets.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.4 states the paper's own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that after the RX encoding the circular data are already separable in the PCA plot, while for the Rot encoding the data are along the same curve, and state that the RX-encoded data can be separated with a quadratic function as discussed in [35].
assertions.anchor: Section 5.4 Role of the encoding, Fig. 6, p.8
quotes: One can see that the circuit data immediately separates for the RX encoding but it does not for the Rot.
coding the data are already separable, contrary to the Rot encoding where the data are along the same curve.
can be separated with a quadratic function as discussed in the work [35]
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one data set.
assertions.reader_inference: Separability is judged visually from a two-component PCA plot; the paper gives no separability measure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Rot-encoded data cannot be separated by a single parameterized processing unitary and would need for example more data re-uploadings.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.4 Role of the encoding, p.8
quotes: cannot be separated by a single parameterized processing unitary and would need for example more data re-uploadings.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper does not train a circuit on the Rot-encoded data in this section.
assertions.reader_inference: The section applies no processing unitary and trains nothing; the statement is inferred from the PCA plot.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results stress the importance of the encoding in a quantum circuit and show that synthetic data sets can favour certain architectures, that if the encoding fails to separate the data the parameterized gates will not be able to separate them on their own, and that the performance of a QP is strongly affected by the encoding and the dataset itself.
quotes: shows that synthetic data sets can favour certain architectures.
the parameterized gates will not be able to separate them on their own.
Therefore, the performance of a QP is strongly affected by the encoding and the dataset itself.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's inference from a PCA illustration on one data set.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [37], that the re-normalization of the data affects the success of training because the quantum functions are periodic, and report that training the deep-teacher students with normalization [−1, 1] instead of [−π, π] gave prediction maps that do not show the whole structure of the data, with both students seeming to perform well.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.4, p.8; Appendix A 4, Fig. 12, p.11
quotes: the re-normalization of the data affects the success of the training, since the quantum functions are periodic and the input data should lie within the period of the function [37]
we train the students in Fig. 3, but with a different normalization, i.e. instead of [−π, π] with [−1, 1].
the prediction maps do not show the whole structure of the data and both students seem to perform well, contrary to Fig. 3 where Student - Re-uploading performs better.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, with a cited explanation [37].
assertions.reader_inference: This is a limit on the paper's own comparison: the RU advantage seen with the [−π, π] grid is not seen with the [−1, 1] normalization.

assertions.value: The authors report that labelling the inner circles of the circular data set with −1 and the outer circles with 1 gave a successful QP student with average ancilla probability vector [0.37, 0.64] for label −1, while the opposite labelling gave a failed training with average probability vector [0.94, 0.06] for label −1, and state that the failure is fixed by adding a PauliX gate before the measurement.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A 3 Labelling matters, Fig. 11, p.11
quotes: the circular data with labels −1 for the inner (black) and 1 for the outer circles (yellow) (Student 1 in Fig. 11)
we get the following average probability vector P−1 = [0.94, 0.06] for the label −1
adding a PauliX gate before the measurement
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The vector [0.37, 0.64] sums to 1.01 as printed, so it is rounded. The prose on p.11 also says 'the prediction map of Student 2 with RX is very different from the circular structure', which conflicts with the caption and the following paragraph where the RX gate fixes Student 2; this is likely a wording slip in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is not sufficient to use deferred measurements to generate hidden non-linearities similar to classical NNs if the output of a QP is reused, and that the expressive power of QNNs only improved when additional data uploadings were added.
quotes: to use deferred measurements to generate hidden non-linearities similar to classical NNs if the output of a QP is reused.
but the expressive power of QNNs only improved when additional datauploadings were added (Fig. 4c).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is still an open question how to build deep QNNs in a coherent way where measurements only occur at the end of the computation, and that one should not expect a one-to-one mapping of quantum and classical NNs.
quotes: it is still an open question how to build deep QNNs in a coherent way, where measurements only occur at the end of the computation.
Thus, one should not expect a one-to-one mapping of quantum and classical NNs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6 states the open problem the paper leaves.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [37], that the number of times that the data are encoded determines the functions that can be approximated, and that the needed non-linearities in a quantum model can be generated, apart from the measurement, from encoding gates that are non-linear functions of the input data.
quotes: These results are in accordance with the recent work [37], which shows that the number of times that the data are encoded determines the functions that can be approximated.
